kernelIdea: "For all" claims something about every case; "there exists" claims at least one case. "There exists exactly one" claims existence and uniqueness.

kernels.l1: Every means check them all. There is one means find just one.
kernels.l2: An every telling talks about all of them, so you have to check them all. A some telling only needs one, so you just have to find one. An exactly one telling needs you to find one and make sure there are no others.
kernels.l3: A for all claim says something about every case, and only a full argument can settle it. A there exists claim says something about at least one case, and a single example settles it. Exactly one claims both that a case exists and that no second case does.
kernels.l4: ∀ claims a property for every element of a stated set; ∃ claims it for at least one; ∃! claims it for one and no more. The quantifier decides what evidence the claim demands.
kernels.l5: Quantifiers turn open statements into statements. ∀x ∈ S, p(x) demands an argument covering all of S; ∃x ∈ S, p(x) is settled by one witness; ∃! adds uniqueness.
kernels.l6: Attaching ∀ or ∃ to a sentence containing a variable turns it into a statement with a definite truth value. Which domain you quantify over is part of the claim, and when quantifiers are nested, so is their order.
kernels.l7: Quantifiers convert predicates into statements: ∀ asserts the predicate on every element of the domain, ∃ on at least one, ∃! on exactly one. The domain is part of the claim, and with nested quantifiers the order is part of the claim too.
kernels.l8: ∀ and ∃ are the infinitary conjunction and disjunction over a domain; quantifier order is the essential content of ε–δ definitions and the difference between pointwise and uniform properties.
